sections.label: Debate on two Bills
sections.summary: Members may raise views on both Bills, with substantive debate held now to avoid duplication, while the Evidence (Amendment) Bill still has its formal Second Reading.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: Members would be welcome to raise questions or express their views on both Bills during this debate.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: But we would still have the formal Second Reading of the Evidence (Amendment) Bill as well, to ensure that procedural requirements are dealt with.

sentences.speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
sentences.text: However, the proposal is to have the substantive debate for both Bills take place now to avoid duplication or overlap, so that all substantive arguments can be captured cogently in a single debate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In 2010, we repealed and re-enacted the Criminal Procedure Code (CPC), after a sustained period of review of more than two years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In 2012, we amended the Evidence Act to reduce the stress that complainants of sexual offences experience during the Court process.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In 2012, we made calibrations to the death penalty regime.

sections.label: Mandatory VRI for rape suspects
sections.summary: In the first phase, VRI is intended to be mandatory for suspects in rape offences under section 375(1)(a) of the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In the first phase of implementation, we intend to make it mandatory to conduct VRI for suspects in rape offences under section 375(1)(a) of the Penal Code.

sections.label: Male officer searching a woman
sections.summary: Amendments allow a male officer to search a woman if he suspects terrorist involvement, believes a terrorist act is imminent, and no woman officer can search in time.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The amendments will allow a male officer to search a woman, in specific circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: These are: first, if the officer reasonably suspects the woman of involvement in a terrorist act; second, the officer believes, in good faith that the terrorist act is imminent; and third, the officer believes, in good faith, that the search cannot be made within a reasonable time by a woman officer.

sections.label: Cheating made non-bailable
sections.summary: Cheating under section 420 of the Penal Code is being made a non-bailable offence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: On that note, we are making certain offences non-bailable: cheating under section 420 of the Penal Code.

sections.label: E-tagging as bail condition
sections.summary: Electronic tagging, or e-tagging, will be allowed as a condition of bail.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Electronic tagging or "e-tagging" will be allowed as a condition of bail.

sections.label: Three new bail offences
sections.summary: The Bill creates three offences: absconding while on bail or personal bond, leaving the jurisdiction without permission, and indemnifying a surety.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Third, the Bill creates three new offences to ensure that bail remains effective.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It will now be an offence to abscond whilst on bail or personal bond; to leave the jurisdiction without permission, for persons whose travel documents have been impounded by investigators; and to indemnify a surety, or, if you are a surety, to agree to be indemnified.

sections.label: Automatic ban on victim identification
sections.summary: Publication of information leading to a victim's identity is automatically prohibited before the case goes to Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: First, the publication of information leading to the victim's identity will be automatically prohibited, even before the case goes before the Courts.

sections.label: Ban on publishing victim identity
sections.summary: Anyone knowing another person is an alleged sexual offence victim cannot publish information that may identify the victim.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Anyone who knows that another person is an alleged victim of a sexual offence will not be allowed to publish any information that may lead to the identification of the victim's identity.

sections.label: Closed-door testimony and Evidence Act
sections.summary: Sexual or child abuse victims testify in closed-door hearings unless they choose open Court, and the Evidence Act will be amended.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Second, all victims of sexual or child abuse offences will give testimony in a closed-door hearing, unless they wish to give evidence in open Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Third, we will amend the Evidence Act so that we can put in place subsidiary legislation that restricts the kinds of questions the Defence can ask.

sections.label: Deferred Prosecution Agreements framework
sections.summary: The Bill introduces a legislative framework for the Prosecution to enter Deferred Prosecution Agreements with corporate offenders.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Bill introduces a legislative framework for the Prosecution to enter into Deferred Prosecution Agreements (DPAs) with corporate offenders.

sections.label: Prosecution agrees not to prosecute
sections.summary: Under a DPA, the Prosecution agrees not to prosecute a corporation in exchange for strict compliance with conditions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Under a DPA, the Prosecution agrees not to prosecute a corporation in exchange for strict compliance by the corporation with a series of conditions.

sections.label: Corporate reform and High Court approval
sections.summary: The corporation may have to implement reform programmes and assist investigations, and all DPAs require High Court approval.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The corporation may also be required to implement programmes for corporate reform going forward and to assist in investigations and prosecution of other wrongdoers, including individuals.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: There are also safeguards: all DPAs will require High Court approval.

sections.label: Criminal Procedure Rules Committee
sections.summary: A Criminal Procedure Rules Committee chaired by the Chief Justice will be established as a structural change to criminal procedure regulation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: A structural change to the way criminal procedure is regulated is that a Criminal Procedure Rules Committee, chaired by the Chief Justice, will be established.

sections.label: Pre-trial disclosure regime coverage
sections.summary: Adding five named Acts means practically all major criminal offences will be covered by the pre-trial disclosure regime.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: With the inclusion of the Prevention of Corruption Act, Moneylenders Act, Remote Gambling Act, Prevention of Human Trafficking Act and Casino Control Act, practically all the major criminal offences will now be covered by the pre-trial disclosure regime for criminal cases.

sections.label: Community sentences and MTO changes
sections.summary: Offenders with prior short imprisonment or reformative training become eligible for community sentences, and MTO scope, duration and in-patient treatment are expanded.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Offenders who have previously served short sentences of imprisonment or previous terms of reformative training will be eligible for community sentences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The MTO will be made available for a prescribed list of more serious offences which are punishable with up to seven years’ imprisonment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Bills also increase the maximum duration of an MTO to 36 months and allow the Court to order a period of in-patient treatment as part of the MTO.

sections.label: Reformative training minimum detention period
sections.summary: The minimum detention period for reformative training will be reduced from 18 months to six or 12 months.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: A key feature of the proposed changes is that the minimum detention period for reformative training will be reduced from 18 months – to six or 12 months, depending on the intensity of the rehabilitation the offender requires.

sections.label: Early release and supervision
sections.summary: New minimum detention periods allow some trainees to be released and placed on supervision as early as the sixth month.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The new minimum detention periods mean that, for some of the trainees, they can be released from detention and placed on supervision as early as the sixth-month mark to begin their reintegration into the community.

sections.label: Court control over re-opening cases
sections.summary: The Bills give the Court more control over applications to re-open concluded criminal cases and similar civil applications.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Bills will give the Court more control over applications to re-open concluded criminal cases where all appeals have been exhausted and civil applications that have a similar effect, by codifying the procedure set out by the Court of Appeal in its recent judgments and providing for other aspects of procedure not covered in previous judgments.

sections.label: Court compensation order process
sections.summary: The Court must give reasons if compensation is not awarded, victims may participate, and dependants may be compensated for bereavement and funeral expenses.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: First, the Court will be required to give reasons if compensation is not awarded, where it has the power to do so.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Second, victims will be able to participate in the compensation order process by making submissions or giving evidence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This is meant for simpler cases – the criminal Courts are simply not equipped to deal with complex hearings usually dealt with by civil Courts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Third, the Court will be empowered to order compensation of the dependants of a person whose death was caused by an offence, for bereavement and funeral expenses.

sections.label: Video-recording accused statements, CCD expansion
sections.summary: The Bill introduces video-recording of accused statements and expands the Criminal Case Disclosure regime, setting the record straight on admissibility issues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: To this end, this Bill introduces video-recording of statements by an accused and expansion of the Criminal Case Disclosure (CCD) regime.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Video-recording of accused's statements sets the record straight with regard to allegations of oppression, inducement, threat or promise – issues that go towards admissibility.

sections.label: Expansion of CCD regime
sections.summary: The expansion of the CCD regime is welcomed because it levels the playing field between prosecution and defence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The expansion of the CCD regime is also welcomed because it levels the playing field between the prosecution and the defence and reduces the perceived advantage a prosecution has in terms of resources and information availability.

sections.label: New section 281B
sections.summary: The new section 281B seeks to reduce the trauma of vulnerable victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Because of this, the new section 281B seeks to reduce the trauma of vulnerable victims.

sections.label: Indemnity agreements and bail sureties
sections.summary: The Member asks the Minister to clarify a possible inconsistency and whether the amendment changes or clarifies the law, and whether prohibiting indemnity agreements removes funding possibilities for families.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: My question is: will the Minister kindly clarify this possible inconsistency – I am not saying that there is an inconsistency, I am saying that there is a possible inconsistency – and whether the amendment is, indeed, changing the law or merely clarifying it?

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: While it is important that sureties' incentive to monitor the accused is not weakened by indemnity, would the prohibition against indemnity agreements remove all possibility for families who would otherwise struggle in getting sufficient funds from getting those funds from relatives and friends so that their loved ones can be released from bail and continue working?

sections.label: Standing and compensation law
sections.summary: The Member asks the Senior Minister of State to clarify whether giving such standing would change the law on compensation to some extent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Will the good Senior Minister of State clarify if she is of the view that giving such standing would change the law on compensation to some extent?

sections.label: Deferred Prosecution Agreement rationale
sections.summary: The passage questions whether an in-house Singapore lawyer is included and argues DPAs must not create misperception that laws are inconsistently applied.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: Just to seek the clarification of the Senior Minister of State, would that include a fully-qualified Singapore lawyer who has now gone in-house, or not?

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: As there is a process of negotiation between the one being sentenced, that is, the company and, on the other hand the prosecutor, as well as opportunity for re-negotiation if the Court fails to approve, it is important that the introduction of the Deferred Prosecution Agreement does not create the misperception that laws will not be consistently applied.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: The Deferred Prosecution Agreement is also a good illustration of the underpinning rationale behind this slew of amendments, that is, not to be content with what we have already achieved but being open to ideas and looking to improve it further, complements what the Senior Minister of State has just said.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: In fact, this was the driving force behind these amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: This is reflected in the title which says, "To enhance the fairness of procedures and ensure correct and equitable outcomes in the criminal justice system".

sentences.speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
sentences.text: That justice is done and is seen to be done is important in a country run on the rule of law.

sections.label: Video-recording of accused statements
sections.summary: Clauses 6 and 7 provide for video-recording of an accused person's statements during an investigation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: First, under clauses 6 and 7, the Bill provides for the video-recording of statements of an accused person during an investigation.

sections.label: Compulsory video-recording Third Schedule offences
sections.summary: Compulsory video-recording applies only to Third Schedule offences, initially only rape cases under section 375(1)(a) of the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The Bill starts small, with compulsory video-recording applicable only to Third Schedule offences which, for a start, will mean only rape cases under section 375(1)(a) of the Penal Code.

sections.label: Low Compensation Order incidences
sections.summary: Parliament previously legislated that judges consider Compensation Orders, but such orders were made in only 48 cases in 2014 and 34 in 2015.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: In the last CPC review, our Parliament legislated that judges who convict offenders should also consider whether to make a Compensation Order for the victim's injuries.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: However, based on the Parliamentary answer in 2016 to a question I filed, the incidences of such Compensation Orders appeared very low, being made in only 48 cases in the year 2014 and 34 cases in 2015.

sections.label: High Court approval of DPAs
sections.summary: The Bill requires all DPAs to be approved by the High Court under the new section 149F of the CPC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: To this end, it is comforting that the Bill will require all DPAs to be approved by the High Court under the new section 149F of the CPC.

sections.label: In camera DPA proceedings
sections.summary: The Bill requires DPA proceedings to be held in camera and does not require the High Court to give reasons for approving a DPA.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: By contrast, the Bill before the House today requires DPA proceedings to be held in camera and does not require the High Court to give any reasons as to why it is approving a DPA.

sections.label: Video link for guilty pleas
sections.summary: The Bill extends video link to guilty plea and sentencing proceedings, raising a concern about whether justice is compromised.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The Bill today seeks to extend video link to proceedings where an accused person pleads guilty and is convicted by a Court and also to proceedings for sentencing after conviction.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: While there is greater security and logistical convenience in using video link in place of physical conveyance of prisoners to Court, I am concerned whether this amendment will compromise justice.

sections.label: Communication confidentiality via telephone link
sections.summary: Communication between the two would occur via telephone or other link, where confidentiality is likely an issue.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: The communication process between the two will be affected as it will need to be done via a telephone or other link where confidentiality is likely to be an issue as well.

sections.label: Clause 7 video-recording rape suspects
sections.summary: The speaker focuses on clause 7, which introduces video-recording of statements by suspects suspected of committing rape.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I will focus on a few proposed amendments which I would like to seek clarifications or re-considerations, after my consultations with some NGOs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I will first start with clause 7 of the Bill which introduces video-recording of statements made by suspects suspected of committing rape.

sections.label: Safeguards for audio-visual recordings
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Minister what safeguards and procedures accompany audio-visual recordings to avoid a misleading account prejudicing the suspect.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As such, I would like to ask the Minister what the other safeguards and procedure are − such as whether the camera will only focus on the suspect person or will also be focused on the interrogators − that will be established, alongside the use of audio-visual recordings' to ensure that the audio-visual recording scheme does not give a misleading account of the suspect which may, in turn, prejudice the suspect.

sections.label: Staged implementation and timelines
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the Government intends to implement the scheme in stages and the related timelines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The first is that I would like to know how the Government intends to implement this scheme in stages and the related timelines for its implementation.

sections.label: Vulnerable victim video-recording discretion
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether an interviewer can decline to video-record a vulnerable victim's statement and record it in writing instead.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Under such circumstances, would the interviewer of a vulnerable victim be able to exercise his or her discretion, even if the Police officer may think it is necessary, to not video-record the statement but instead record it in writing under the proposed section 22(5)(c)?

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I hope that the Ministry can set out how it seeks to address such a situation where the victim might feel very uncomfortable to go on video to record his or her statement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I turn now to clause 78 of the Bill which proposes that psychiatrists will only be allowed to give expert evidence in criminal cases if they are on a Court-administered panel of psychiatrists.

sections.label: One review application limit
sections.summary: Proposed section 394K provides that an applicant cannot make more than one review application to re-open an appellate Court decision.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The first is regarding the proposed section 394K which provides that the applicant cannot make more than one review application in respect of re-opening a decision of an appellate Court.

sections.label: Sufficient material for review
sections.summary: Proposed section 394J requires the applicant to satisfy the Court there is sufficient material to conclude a miscarriage of justice occurred.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The second concern I have is with the proposed section 394J of the Bill which provides that the applicant in a review application must satisfy the Court that there is sufficient material on which the appellate Court may conclude that there has been a miscarriage of justice in the criminal matter.

sections.label: Finality versus miscarriage of justice
sections.summary: The speaker says finality must not preclude rectifying miscarriages, and cites Yong Vui Kong v State on floodgates arguments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But such finality must not come at the expense of rigid rules precluding the Court from rectifying potential miscarriages of justice.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Also, while I understand that the high threshold standard set out in the proposed section 394J is also to keep the "floodgates" of unmeritorious cases shut, but, as the words of the Court of Appeal, in the case of Yong Vui Kong v State, I quote, "the floodgates arguments should not be allowed to wash away both the guilty and the innocent".

sections.label: Protecting sexual assault victims
sections.summary: The speaker urges more restrictions on cross-examination, a Court duty to prevent re-victimisation, and sensitivity training for defence lawyers.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I cannot imagine being a woman trying to bring her rapist to justice in Courtrooms where these kinds of arguments are used." Her powerful sharing reminds us of how victims really need to be protected with great sensitivity and care.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I wish the amendment would go further in putting more restrictions in how cross-examination should be done.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Court must have a duty to ensure that victims are not re-victimised, being asked questions which are unduly annoying, harassing, intimidating, offensive, oppressive, humiliating or repetitive, or has no basis other than a stereotype.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I also would like to suggest that defence lawyers be encouraged or required to attend some training to sensitise them to what sexual assault victims go through before they take on such cases.

sentences.speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Insensitive cross-examination not only hurts the victim on the stand, but also deters others from bringing their case forward.

sections.label: Video-recorded statements benefits
sections.summary: Video-recorded statements aim to safeguard accused persons' rights, protect officers from baseless accusations, reduce Court time and reduce victims' trauma.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The move to allow video-recorded statements heeds the longstanding calls from the legal fraternity and fellow colleagues for the use of video-recording by law enforcement officers when taking statements from accused persons and witnesses.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The use of video-recorded statements aims to better safeguard the rights of accused persons in the process of taking their statements, go some way towards protecting the officers who are taking the statements against baseless accusations that they had coerced or threatened the witness and help to reduce the Court time spent on unmeritorious challenges as to the voluntariness of the statements given in the Police interviews.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Video-recorded statements can also help to reduce the trauma faced by vulnerable victims of crime in having to recount their ordeal repeatedly through the investigation process by using the video-recorded statements as their oral evidence-in-chief in Court.

sections.label: No defence access to recordings
sections.summary: The Ministry shared that copies of video-recorded statements will not be given to the defence due to risk of online posting or black market sale.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The Ministry has also shared that copies of the video-recorded statements will not be made available to the defence due to the risk of recordings being posted online or sold on the black market.

sections.label: Bail regime amendments welcomed
sections.summary: The amendments to strengthen the bail regime are welcomed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The amendments to strengthen the bail regime are welcomed.

sections.label: Mandatory Treatment Order eligibility expansion
sections.summary: The Bill expands MTO eligibility to prescribed offences carrying up to seven years' imprisonment and raises the maximum MTO duration from 24 to 36 months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The Bill seeks to expand the eligibility for Mandatory Treatment Orders (MTO) to include offenders who commit certain prescribed offences carrying up to seven years' imprisonment from the current three years and the maximum duration of the MTO sentences increased from 24 to 36 months.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The amendments will also allow the Court to order the offender to reside at the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) for a specified duration of in-patient treatment as a condition of the MTO.

sections.label: Deferred prosecution agreements certainty transparency
sections.summary: Certainty and transparency must be ensured so DPAs are not perceived as a way for corporations to game the system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: With regard to the introduction of DPAs, certainty and transparency must be ensured so that DPAs are not perceived as a way for corporations to game the system.

sections.label: Restricting questions on sexual history
sections.summary: The amendment seeks to restrict the defence from asking complainants questions or adducing evidence on their sexual history or activities without the Court's leave.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: MinLaw has shared that the amendment to the Act seeks to restrict the defence from asking complainants questions or adduce evidence concerning their sexual history or activities, including their appearance or behaviour, other than those to which the charge related, without the leave of the Court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Such leave will only be granted if it would be in the interests of justice to allow the question to be asked or the evidence to be adduced.

sections.label: Guidelines for child abuse sexual offences
sections.summary: Practice directions or guidelines should be formulated setting out the approach prosecutors and defence counsel should take in handling child abuse and sexual offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Second, a set of practice directions or guidelines should be formulated to set out the approach prosecutors and defence counsel should take in handling child abuse and sexual offences.

sections.label: Best practices for defence counsel
sections.summary: The guidelines should set out best practices for defence counsel to refrain from unnecessary lines of questioning and assertions against victims.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The set of guidelines should draw reference from these cases and set out best practices for defence counsel to adopt in formulating their case theory, to refrain from subjecting the victims to such unnecessary lines of questioning and assertions where such assertions do not mitigate or justify the accused's conduct or diminish the complainant's credibility.

sections.label: Guidelines for cross-examining vulnerable witnesses
sections.summary: Guidelines should cover defence cross-examination of child and vulnerable witnesses, using simple questions to elicit accurate evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: Besides these guidelines, the set of guidelines should also include best practices on how defence counsel should shape their cross-examination strategy in respect of child witnesses or witnesses of lower intellectual abilities, bearing in mind the general rule of practice which has been affirmed by the Court of Appeal in BMD v Public Prosecutor, that the evidence of such a witness is generally not taken at face value as such witnesses may find it difficult to distinguish between reality and fantasy, and between results of observation and results of imagination.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The guidelines should also include best practices on how the defence counsel should put their case to victims in child abuse and sexual offences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: On the defence counsel’s part, care should be taken to formulate questions to suit the witness’ level of understanding, such as through the use of short and simple questions, given that the language used conventionally by counsel in putting their cases tends to be complex and certain classes of vulnerable witnesses may be highly susceptible to suggestion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
sentences.text: The aim of the defence counsel should be to elicit the most accurate evidence that the vulnerable witness is able to give rather than to confuse or confound the witness to give an impression of a lack of credibility.

sections.label: Video-recording of offence categories
sections.summary: Video-recording under new section 225B is welcomed, starting with certain offence categories, with hope it becomes the norm.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Video-recording or the new section 225B is welcomed because – it begins with certain categories of offences – the hope is that, in time, video-recording may become a norm as it is in other jurisdictions, including the UK.

sections.label: Access to video copy
sections.summary: A question is asked whether there is a principled reason the video copy is not furnished to defence counsel and the accused.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, I ask a very technical and procedural point: even though there is going to be video-recording, is there a significant, principled reason as to why this particular copy of the video will not be furnished to defence counsel and the accused person himself or herself?

sections.label: Reviewing footage and evidence-in-chief substitution
sections.summary: The Minister is asked to confirm defence counsel can review footage repeatedly, and concerns are raised about video substituting evidence-in-chief.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Putting aside the additional resource burden that this will place on the Police to make such arrangements for defence lawyers to view the video footage, could the Minister confirm, for the record, that defence counsel will be able to review the footage as many times that they may want to and at a time of mutual convenience to the Police and to them?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Separately, looking at section 264A that is being proposed and here I am looking at statements recorded through video as well, at the suggestion that, in certain situations, video-recordings may even be used as a substitute or as a complement to evidence that is given in-chief in Court – the Criminal Bar, during consultations, has expressed legitimate concerns about the implications on the trial process if video-recordings are used, even partially, to substitute evidence-in-chief in Court.

sections.label: Codifying the Kho Jiabing test
sections.summary: The current law codifies the Court of Appeal position in Kho Jiabing, described as the Kho Jiabing-plus test in statute.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The Senior Minister of State said earlier that it is codified, the current law, and she is correct because it codifies the position that was taken in Kho Jiabing by the Court of Appeal.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But in doing so actually looking at the test in statute, hard coded in statute and noting that she mentioned earlier that it is that test in Kho Jiabing-plus, which is how I refer to this test, Kho Jiabing-plus.

sections.label: PP v Mohamed Ariffan CLAS case
sections.summary: In the 2018 High Court case Public Prosecutor v Mohamed Ariffan, a CLAS case, the defendant was acquitted of rape and sexual violence charges.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The 2018 case of Public Prosecutor v Mohamed Ariffan, which was a Criminal Legal Aid Scheme (CLAS) case ‒ that was argued before the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And at the High Court, the defendant was acquitted of charges, including rape and sexual violence.

sections.label: Court of Appeal evidence ruling
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal said legal tests will not change but admitted some evidence as useful for the appeal.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: So, the natural question is why should such evidence be relevant or even necessary?

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: And the issues were argued extensively and, ultimately, the Court of Appeal said the legal tests will not be changed, but, having said that, there would be some evidence which would be useful in their determination of that case on appeal and admitted some parts of the evidence.

sections.label: Court caution on wrongful conviction
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal said courts are anxious not to convict the innocent or impose disproportionate sentences.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In that case, while it is important, the Court of Appeal reminded us there is dire anxiety on the part of the Court not to convict an innocent person or to impose a sentence that is out of proportion to the criminality of the offenders, they tread very carefully to avoid any prejudice that could be suffered by an accused person who is wrongly convicted or who receives a manifestly disproportionate sentence relevant to their culpability.

sections.label: Criticism of cross-examination overstepping
sections.summary: Colleagues criticised cross-examination that oversteps the bounds.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The criticism that came from my fellow colleagues was about cross-examination that oversteps the bounds.

sections.label: Chilling effect on defence lawyers
sections.summary: Questions did not stray beyond a line, but the speaker asks whether lawyers would be deterred from asking questions.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Questions never went or strayed beyond a particular line; never were inappropriate.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: But do we want to have a chilling effect on responsible defence lawyers, Mr Speaker to tell them to not just be careful but, maybe, do not ask a particular question?

sections.label: Support for the Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Bill notwithstanding the points raised.

sentences.speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With that, and notwithstanding those points, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Sexual assault reformative training sentence
sections.summary: An individual was convicted of sexual assault and rape of a 16-year-old girl and sentenced to reformative training.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In this case, an individual was convicted for sexual assault and rape of a 16-year-old girl and sentenced to reformative training.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: There are some who may consider this a light sentence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: They may change their mind when they learn that the offender was 14 years old when he committed the offence and has a low IQ of 61.

sections.label: Prosecution sought jail and caning
sections.summary: The prosecution asked for a jail term of 15 to 18 years with at least 15 strokes of the cane.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The prosecution asked for a jail term of between 15 and 18 years with at least 15 strokes of the cane.

sections.label: Justice Woo on sentencing issues
sections.summary: Justice Woo said the case exposed larger issues, including limited sentencing options for a young offender with some intellectual disability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Ultimately, Justice Woo had said that this case had exposed larger issues at stake, including limited sentencing options available to a Court faced with a young offender who has some intellectual disability.

sections.label: Video-recording interview regulations guidelines
sections.summary: The question asks if the Senior Minister of State will consider requiring the entire interview to be recorded and barring unrecorded pre-interrogation exchanges or preliminary interviews except where absolutely necessary.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will the Senior Minister of State consider including in regulations or guidelines on the use of video-recording the requirement that the entire interview must be recorded and that the Police do not engage in unrecorded pre-interrogation exchanges or preliminary interviews with the suspect except where absolutely necessary?

sections.label: Mandatory video-recording for vulnerable suspects
sections.summary: The question asks if the Minister will consider making video-recordings mandatory for all offences punishable with death or life imprisonment and for all vulnerable suspects, regardless of the alleged offence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will the Minister consider making video-recordings mandatory for all offences punishable with death or life imprisonment and for all vulnerable suspects, including juveniles, the elderly, the cognitively impaired or the psychologically disordered, regardless of the alleged offence?

sections.label: Scope of proposed section 154A
sections.summary: The question asks what questions proposed section 154A(1)(a) will cover that do not already fall under section 154.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can I clarify what questions the proposed section 154A(1)(a) will cover that do not already fall under the scope of section 154?

sections.label: Offence of a sexual nature
sections.summary: The question asks the Senior Minister of State to clarify that an offence will not be deemed sexual just because it falls under section 356.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify that an offence will not be deemed to be of a sexual nature just because it falls under section 356?

sections.label: Expanding community-based sentencing to fine offences
sections.summary: The proposed amendments take up the suggestion to expand community-based sentencing to offences with specified minimum fines.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The present proposed amendments go towards this and I am glad to see that my suggestion to expand community-based sentencing (CBS) to offences with specified minimum sentences of fine has been taken up.

sections.label: Spent records for community sentences
sections.summary: Under the Registration of Criminals Act, a record for a crime given a community sentence is deemed spent upon completion of the sentence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Under the registration of Criminals Act, the record for crime for which a community sentence was imposed by the Court will be deemed spent upon completion of the sentence.

sections.label: Twelve-month mandatory treatment order imposed
sections.summary: The Court imposed a 12-month mandatory treatment order on her.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Court imposed a 12-month MTO on her.

sections.label: Limits on community-based sentencing eligibility
sections.summary: Community-based sentencing remains unavailable to persons who committed serious offences with fixed or mandatory minimum imprisonment sentences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The stipulation that CBS is not available to persons who have committed serious offences for which sentences are fixed by law or prescribed by a mandatory minimum sentence of imprisonment or an offence for which the sentence is fixed by law still remains.

sections.label: Psychiatrist's sole judgement in mandatory treatment orders
sections.summary: The speaker says the Court's determination for mandatory treatment orders is constrained by the sole professional judgement of the appointed psychiatrist.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This being the case for reformative training sentences, it is, with respect, incongruent that, for MTOs, the Court's determination is constrained by the sole professional judgement of the appointed psychiatrist.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I personally dealt with a case where a psychiatrist issued an opinion supporting an imposition of an MTO on my client who was suffering from an anti-personality disorder, which I understand, requires intensive in-patient treatment for a significant period of time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This opinion was used to persuade the Court to call for a suitability assessment for an MTO.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The same psychiatrist was then appointed by the Director and, later on, he issued a diametrically opposed opinion without providing sufficient explanation for the change in opinion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The Court was not in a position to look beyond the second opinion based on the current provisions.

sections.label: Deferred prosecution agreement regime introduced
sections.summary: The Criminal Justice Reform Bill introduces deferred prosecution agreements, approved by the High Court, allowing prosecution and corporation to make submissions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Third, the Criminal Justice Reform Bill introduces the deferred prosecution agreement regime, which allows the prosecution to enter into an agreement with the accused corporation to agree not to prosecute, in exchange for compliance with a series of conditions, such as payment of a financial penalty, or the appointment of a person to assess and monitor the corporation’s internal controls.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The contemplated DPA regime requires that DPAs are approved by the High Court and allows for the prosecution and corporation that is the subject of the DPA to make submissions before the Court makes its determination.

sections.label: Interested parties in DPA hearings
sections.summary: A question asks whether the DPA regime precludes the Court from letting interested stakeholders join proceedings before approving a DPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The present DPA regime does not appear to allow for the intervention of such interested parties at the hearing by the Court to determine whether or not to approve the DPA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: Would the hon Senior Minister of State please clarify that the provisions do not preclude the Court from allowing interested stakeholders to join in the proceedings so that it is in a position to properly consider the interests of all the relevant stakeholders or parties before approving the DPA?

sections.label: Protection for abuse victims
sections.summary: Proposed amendments seek to reduce stress for sexual or child abuse victims, citing UK restrictions on sexual history evidence and proposed section 154A of the Evidence Act.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The proposed amendments seek to enhance the protection for victims of sexual or child abuse, to reduce the stress they may face in the criminal justice process.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For example, in the UK, section 41 of the Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act imposes a general prohibition on the admission of evidence or questions in cross-examination relating to the sexual history of a complainant, save in narrow exceptions, such as where the evidence is necessary to rebut prosecution evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: However, even where one of the exceptions is met, the judge must be satisfied that further criteria are met, such as that the purpose of the evidence is not to impugn the complainant’s credibility and the evidence is required to ensure a fair trial.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The UK process requires the defence to obtain the Court’s permission to introduce such questions or evidence about a complainant’s sexual history, by way of an application made to Court within a specific timeframe, according to requirements set out in the UK Criminal Procedure Rules.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
sentences.text: In our case, the proposed section 154A of the Evidence Act provides that the Minister may make rules to restrict the questions that may be asked of an alleged victim of cross-examination.

sections.label: Video-link hearings expansion
sections.summary: The passage states the first item is the expansion of video-link hearings for pleas of guilt and sentencing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: First, the expansion of video-link hearings for pleas of guilt and sentencing.

sections.label: Video recording of interviews
sections.summary: The passage states that allowing video recording of interviews and suspects' statements lets Courts try cases more effectively through a contemporaneous account.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Second, allowing video recording of the interviews and suspects’ statements will allow the Courts to try cases more effectively by providing a contemporaneous account of the interview.

sections.label: Protecting alleged victim identity
sections.summary: The passage states the proposal will protect the identity of an alleged victim even before a charge is tendered.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The proposal will protect the identity of an alleged victim even before a charge is tendered.

sections.label: Victim identity and closed-door evidence
sections.summary: The passage states victims' identities will be protected, they can give evidence in closed-door hearings, and screens will prevent them seeing attackers.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: With the amendments, victims can be assured that their identities will be protected.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: In addition, they will be able to give their evidence in a closed-door hearing.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: The Bill will also allow for the use of screens that will prevent victims from having to see their attackers.

sections.label: Court permission for sexual history questions
sections.summary: MinLaw announced that under these rules the Court's permission is required before asking a victim questions about sexual history unrelated to the charge.

sentences.speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
sentences.text: MinLaw has announced that under these rules, the Court's permission will be required before the victim can be asked questions about their sexual history that do not relate to the charge.

sections.label: Subsidiary legislation on expert evidence
sections.summary: The proposed amendments will allow subsidiary legislation on expert evidence, including expert obligations, concurrent expert evidence known as hot-tubbing, and joint expert reports.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The proposed amendments will allow subsidiary legislation on the use of expert evidence, including the obligations of evidence and the use of concurrent expert evidence, which have been colloquially described in some jurisdictions as "hot-tubbing", or the use of what they call, joint expert reports.

sections.label: Court of Appeal suggests hot-tubbing
sections.summary: In a Mental Capacity Act case, the Court of Appeal suggested medical expert evidence ideally be tested through hot-tubbing and that extending this to criminal hearings could benefit.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: In a recent case involving an application under the Mental Capacity Act for a declaration that a woman was unable to make decisions on her property and affairs because of a mental impairment, the Court of Appeal suggested in a postscript that, ideally, medical expert evidence in such cases should be tested through "hot-tubbing" and there can be benefits to extending this procedure to criminal hearings.

sections.label: Consult professional bodies before regulations
sections.summary: Each expert domain has its own professional practice for complex cases, so relevant professional bodies should be consulted before the regulations are enacted.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: Thirdly, in particular, each expert domain – whether engineers, computer security, medical professionals – each will have its own established professional practice for discussion of complex expert cases.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: So there should be consultation with the relevant professional bodies before the regulations are enacted.

sections.label: Maximum confinement for unfit persons
sections.summary: The Bill sets a maximum duration for the Minister's confinement order over persons unfit to plead, with medical opinion, judicial safeguards and community care recognised.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: For example, the existing section 249(2) allows the Minister discretion to confine a person of unsound mind who is unfit to plead, but does not specify an upper limit as to how long this confinement might be.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: The amendments in this Bill set out a maximum duration for the Minister's order of confinement over such persons and will help ensure that such persons are not confined under the criminal law for longer than a person in a similar position without a mental condition affecting fitness to plead.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: However, there is a clarification as well to ask the Minister: what happens when the maximum term of confinement under the CPC has been reached and the subject is still found to be unsafe for discharge because he or she remains a danger to themselves or others?

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: They allow for a greater role for modern medical opinion, and additional judicial safeguards.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
sentences.text: They reflect a more enlightened attitude towards those with mental conditions, as they recognise that, with proper supervision and the right conditions, some such persons can safely be cared for in the community.

sections.label: Balance accuser confrontation and victim protection
sections.summary: The amendments balance giving an accused the chance to confront his accuser with protecting victims from uncontrolled, unnecessary and humiliating questions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The amendments strike a proper balance between two objectives: the objective of ensuring that an accused person is given the opportunity to confront his or her accuser, and the objective of protecting victims from uncontrolled, unnecessary and humiliating questions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The possibility of having to put up with the humiliating and sometimes cruel scrutiny from the lawyers is a common reason why sexual assault victims do not report the crime.

sections.label: Video-recorded statements replace oral testimony
sections.summary: Using video-recorded statements instead of oral testimony means victims need not retell their horrific experience during examination-in-chief.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The use of video-recorded statements in lieu of oral testimony is good because this will mean that victims will not be required to retell their horrific experience during their examination-in-chief.

sections.label: MTOs treat offending behaviour
sections.summary: MTOs address the root of the offending behaviour by ensuring such individuals receive treatment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: MTOs address the root of the offending behaviour by ensuring that such individuals receive treatment.

sections.label: Bill changes criminal procedure
sections.summary: The Bill makes wide-ranging criminal procedure changes: greater investigative transparency, better victim protection, more whistle-blower incentives, and improvements in the process before the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
sentences.text: The Ministry had said that community-based sentences have been frequently imposed and have been successful in achieving their objectives.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: This Bill makes important and wide-ranging changes in criminal procedure, which will enhance the administration of justice in a variety of ways: first, it provides greater transparency in the investigative and evidence-gathering process; second, it provides better protection for victims of crimes; third, it provides more incentives for whistle-blowers to come forward; and fourth, it makes important improvements in the process before the Courts.

sections.label: Amendments make Court process less intimidating
sections.summary: Steps can reduce fear, and the Act's amendments make the Court process less intimidating for the victim, hopefully without compromising the accused's opportunity to challenge their evidence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: But what we can do is to take what steps we can to reduce that fear.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: And a number of the important amendments in this Act include the amendments to make the Court process less intimidating for the victim, though, hopefully, not compromising the opportunity for the accused to challenge their evidence.

sections.label: Commercial incentives encourage whistle-blowing
sections.summary: The logic of the details is simple and the commercial incentives it intends to promote basically support and encourage whistle-blowing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The logic of the details is quite simple and I think the commercial incentives it intends to promote is this: it is basically to support and encourage whistle-blowing.

sections.label: Court approval and publication keep transparency
sections.summary: The requirement for Court approval and publication of the delay also keeps the process transparent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: The requirement for Court approval and publication of the delay also keeps the process transparent.

sections.label: Deferred prosecution agreements for corporate crimes
sections.summary: The DPA is a tool for the prosecution to deal with corporate crimes, and the Court need not give reasons for approving it.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: On the whole, the DPA is an interesting tool to give to the prosecution and this should enable them to deal particularly with corporate crimes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: There is no requirement for the Court to give reasons for approving the DPA.

sections.label: Limiting re-opening to single application
sections.summary: Most key amendments reflect existing Court of Appeal positions, except limiting re-opening to a single application, and the reason for this one-bite rule is asked.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Most key amendments appear to be what are the positions taken by the Court of Appeal already, save for one, and that is the limiting of re-opening to a single application.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: What is the reason for this one-bite rule?

sections.label: Safeguards against unmeritorious prosecutions
sections.summary: It asks whether safeguards exist for defendants to filter out unmeritorious prosecutions early rather than only after an extensive hearing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Are there any safeguards in place for defendants to filter out unmeritorious prosecutions at an early stage, rather than only after an extensive hearing?

sections.label: Police training for camera statements
sections.summary: The Police have a four-day training programme for taking statements on camera, covering interview skills, administrative procedures and tackling equipment failure.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Police have a training programme in place, for taking statements while on camera.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: They go through a four-day course which includes interview skills, administrative procedures in conducting a video interview and how to tackle equipment failure.

sections.label: Viewing video statements at designated locations
sections.summary: Defence Counsel may view video-recorded statements only at designated locations, where recording devices are not allowed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Viewing of the video-recorded statements by Defence Counsel will only be allowed at designated locations, where recording devices will not be allowed.

sections.label: Safeguard against misuse of video-recordings
sections.summary: This safeguards against misuse of video-recordings; instead of a copy, Defence Counsel may view the recording at an approved place any number of times.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, this is really to make sure that there is a safeguard against the video-recordings being misused.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: However, instead of handing over a copy of the video-recorded interview, Defence Counsel would be able to view the recording at an approved place any number of times.

sections.label: Cameras in statement-taking room
sections.summary: Two cameras will be mounted in the room, one focusing on the interviewee and the other capturing an overview of the entire room.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng also asked whether the Government would consider requiring the video footage to show both the suspect and statement taker, as well as the full extent of the space in the room, and Mr Kok Heng Leun expressed a similar concern on capturing the suspect’s demeanour accurately.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: There will be two cameras mounted in the room, one of which focuses on the interviewee and the other captures an overview of the entire room.

sections.label: Training investigating officers for VRI
sections.summary: Investigating officers need training because the statement-taking methodology changes as there will be no written statement if a VRI is recorded.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Investigating officers need to be trained as the entire statement-taking methodology changes because there will no longer be any written statement, if a VRI is to be recorded.

sections.label: Trained officers take victims' statements
sections.summary: Specially trained Police officers are expected to take video-recorded statements from such victims, though operational details are not yet worked out.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: While the operational details are yet to be worked out, we expect that specially trained Police officers will take the video-recorded statements from such victims.

sections.label: Investigators decide statement mode
sections.summary: Investigators will make a decision on the mode of taking the statement.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Investigators will make a decision on the mode of taking the statement.

sections.label: Factors in recording mode decision
sections.summary: The investigator will take into account the victim's preference and his or her composure or state of mind when deciding the appropriate mode of recording.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The victim’s preference and his/her composure or state of mind at the time of statement-taking will be taken into account by the investigator in deciding on the appropriate mode of recording.

sections.label: Female suicide bomber attacks
sections.summary: Between 1985 and 2008, female suicide bombers carried out more than 230 attacks, about a quarter of all such acts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Between 1985 and 2008, female suicide bombers carried out more than 230 attacks, about a quarter of all such acts.

sections.label: Boko Haram female suicide bombers
sections.summary: Female suicide bombers deployed by Boko Haram have killed more than 1,225 people.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Female suicide bombers deployed by Boko Haram have killed more than 1,225 people.

sections.label: Male officers searching women
sections.summary: Male officers will only be allowed to search a woman in very narrowly defined circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In our case, as mentioned, male officers will only be allowed to search a woman in very narrowly defined circumstances.

sections.label: Absconding from bail offence
sections.summary: Absconding from bail will be made an offence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In particular, absconding from bail will be made an offence.

sections.label: First Schedule sexual abuse offences
sections.summary: The First Schedule currently lists the main sexual and child abuse offences that are more frequently prosecuted.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The First Schedule, currently, lists the main sexual and child abuse offences that are more frequently prosecuted.

sections.label: Penal Code Review Committee
sections.summary: A Penal Code Review Committee has been set up to conduct a broad review of the Penal Code and will make recommendations this year.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Government has announced this before and I will emphasise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: There is a Penal Code Review Committee that has been set up to conduct a broad review of the Penal Code.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Committee will complete its work and make its recommendations sometime this year.

sections.label: Questions about victim's sexual behaviour
sections.summary: The accused or his Counsel cannot ask questions about a victim's sexual behaviour with persons other than the accused when unrelated to the charge, unless leave of Court is obtained.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: As explained, the accused or his Counsel will not be allowed to ask questions about a victim’s sexual behaviour with persons other than the accused when such behaviour does not relate to the charge, unless leave of Court is first obtained.

sections.label: Restricting cross-examination questions of alleged victims
sections.summary: The measures allow the Minister to make rules restricting questions asked of alleged victims in cross-examination, including requiring the Court's permission for certain questions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The measures that we are putting in place today will further strengthen these safeguards by allowing the Minister to make rules to further restrict the kinds of questions that can be asked of alleged victims during cross-examination, including the introduction of a requirement to ask the Court's permission before certain questions are asked.

sections.label: Confinement after CPC maximum term
sections.summary: If the maximum CPC confinement term is reached and the subject remains unsafe, he or she moves to the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act regime and continues confinement for treatment, usually at IMH.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Dr Tan Wu Meng asked about what would happen if the maximum term of confinement under the CPC has been reached and the subject is still found to be unsafe for discharge as he or she remains a danger to himself or herself or others.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: He or she will be transited to the regime under the Mental Health (Care and Treatment) Act and will continue to be confined for treatment, usually at the IMH.

sections.label: No publication of prosecutorial guidelines
sections.summary: The answer is no, as publishing prosecutorial guidelines would differ from the UK approach and could let criminals manipulate the criminal justice system to escape punishment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The answer is, no, because that would be similar to publishing prosecutorial guidelines and we have a slightly different approach from that of the UK.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In Singapore, the general position on such publication is different.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This is to ensure that prosecutorial guidelines do not become a tool for criminals to refer to in manipulating the criminal justice system to escape punishment.

sections.label: Approval threshold for deferred prosecution agreements
sections.summary: Approval is granted only if the DPA is in the interests of justice and its terms are fair, reasonable and proportionate, and the Court must not approve it otherwise.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The approval will only be granted if the DPA is in the interests of justice and its terms are fair, reasonable and proportionate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Court should not grant or approve the DPA unless it has met that threshold.

sections.label: Extending pre-trial disclosure regime
sections.summary: Today's amendments extend the pre-trial disclosure regime to cover practically every criminal offence likely to be tried at the High Court.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Today's amendments extend the pre-trial disclosure regime to cover practically every criminal offence that is likely to be tried at the High Court.

sections.label: Cross-examination rarely invoked, discovery kept
sections.summary: Statistics show the cross-examination part is very rarely invoked, but the discovery part will be kept.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: What the statistics have shown is that the cross-examination part of it is very rarely invoked but we will, of course, keep the discovery part.

sections.label: Prison tele-visit for counsel
sections.summary: Prisons run a tele-visit system letting counsel interview remand clients by teleconferencing without travelling to the prison.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The Prisons currently operate a tele-visit system that allows counsel to interview their clients in remand through teleconferencing without physically travelling to the prison.

sections.label: Section 27 PCA statement admissibility
sections.summary: Section 27 PCA statements are admissible only if there is no inducement, threat or promise and the taker believed in good faith the interviewee was concerned in a PCA offence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Statements taken under section 27 of the PCA will only be admissible as evidence in the trial of that person for any criminal offence, in the following circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: There is no inducement, threat or promise that would otherwise render the statement inadmissible; and the person taking the statement under section 27 of the PCA must have believed, in good faith, that the interviewee was a person who had been concerned in any offence under the PCA.

sections.label: Safeguards for CPIB statements
sections.summary: Safeguards require a CPIB officer to believe in good faith the interviewee was concerned in a PCA offence before using the statement to prosecute other offences.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: To prevent that, we have inserted the safeguards earlier mentioned: it requires that the CPIB officer can only use the statement in the prosecution of other offences, when he or she believes in good faith that the interviewee was a person who had been concerned in any offence under PCA.

sections.label: Telling person to tell truth
sections.summary: The amendment clarifies that telling a person he is legally bound to tell the truth does not by itself make a statement inadmissible.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The amendment, therefore, clarifies that, on its own, telling a person that he is legally bound to tell the truth, shall not render a statement inadmissible.

sections.label: Community sentence recidivism data
sections.summary: Early data suggests offenders given community sentences tend to have a lower recidivism rate than the general prison population.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Having said that, early data suggests that the recidivism rate amongst offenders sentenced to community sentences tend to have a lower rate of recidivism than the general prison population.

sections.label: Expanded MTO offence list
sections.summary: The expanded list of offences eligible for MTOs under the revised criteria will be clearly set out in legislation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The expanded list of offences which will be eligible for MTOs under the revised criteria will be clearly set out in legislation.

sections.label: IMH conflict of medical ethics
sections.summary: IMH is generally the institution administering MTO treatment, raising concern of conflict of medical ethics if asked to treat a person it believes has no treatable mental condition.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Given that, generally, IMH is the institution to administer treatment under the MTO, there is a concern of conflict of medical ethics if IMH were to be asked to treat a person it believes does not have a treatable mental condition.

sections.label: Amendments expand MTO eligibility
sections.summary: The amendments significantly expand the range of offenders potentially eligible for MTOs, which is hoped to address Mr Murali Pillai's concerns.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In the meantime, the amendments today significantly expand the range of offenders potentially eligible for MTOs and we hope that this will go some way to addressing Mr Murali Pillai's concerns.

sections.label: MHA review on sentencing
sections.summary: MHA will consider Mr Murali Pillai's noted case in the context of a broader policy review on sentencing.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Mr Murali Pillai made a similar observation about the limitations in that case.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: We have taken note of this case and MHA will consider this in the context of a broader policy review on sentencing.

sections.label: No statutory compensation limit
sections.summary: There is no statutory limit on the amount of compensation that can be ordered.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether there would be a limit on the amount of compensation awarded.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: There is no statutory limit on the compensation that can be ordered.

sections.label: Compensation limited to funeral expenses
sections.summary: Criminal compensation for a deceased victim's dependants has been limited to funeral expenses and bereavement because these are easily quantified and assessed.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Criminal compensation for a deceased victim’s dependants has been limited to funeral expenses and bereavement because these expenditures are easily quantified and assessed.

sections.label: Standard for miscarriage of justice review
sections.summary: Parties must make all reasonable efforts to find relevant evidence, and the material must be compelling, reliable, substantial and powerfully probative to show a miscarriage of justice.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Obviously, that is to impress upon parties that they must take all reasonable efforts to look for the relevant evidence.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And the material must be compelling, in that the material is reliable, substantial, powerfully probative and capable of showing almost conclusively that there has been a miscarriage of justice in the criminal matter in respect of which the earlier decision was made.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This is repeated in other provisions where it says that the appellate Court may conclude there has been a miscarriage of justice in the criminal matter if the earlier decision is demonstrably wrong and the earlier decision is tainted by fraud or breach of rules on a matter of justice, such that the integrity of the judicial process is compromised.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: It is not sufficient to show that there was a real possibility that the earlier decision is wrong; it must be apparent based on the evidence tendered in support of the review application that there is a powerful probability that the earlier decision is wrong.

sections.label: Appellate court inherent review power
sections.summary: The amendments do not affect an appellate Court's inherent power to review its own earlier decision on its own motion.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: In that scenario, it is actually provided for – because the amendments provide that it does not affect the inherent power of an appellate Court to review on its own motion an earlier decision of the appellate Court.

sections.label: Preventing defence trial ambush
sections.summary: The aim is to prevent the defence from ambushing the prosecution by producing documentary exhibits only at trial, which causes adjournments and follow-up investigations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The idea here is you also do not want to allow the defence to ambush the prosecution by only producing its documentary exhibits at trial because that really does not save resources as well and then it results in adjournments and follow-up investigations and so on.

sections.label: Restrictions placed in subsidiary legislation
sections.summary: The restrictions were placed in subsidiary legislation after discussions with the Law Society to allow greater flexibility for refinements balancing due process and preventing victim trauma.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The decision to place the restrictions in subsidiary legislation was made pursuant to discussions with the Law Society as it was thought that this would allow for greater flexibility to make refinements over time to strike a fair balance between due process and preventing trauma to the victim.

sections.label: Minister formulating question restrictions
sections.summary: The Minister was decided to be best placed to consider the wide spectrum of interests in formulating restrictions on questions, and will consult all affected parties including the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The specific restrictions on questions have to be formulated in consideration of a very wide spectrum of interests that may go beyond the expertise of the CPRC.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: For example, the views of those who work closely with victims of sexual offences would be relevant.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: So, on balance, we decided that the Minister would, for now, be best placed to consider the entire spectrum of considerations.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But, of course, the Minister will consult all affected parties, including the Courts, when formulating these restrictions.      .
